Features OSINT reputation evidence from public sources: VirusTotal (domain and relations), MXToolbox blacklist check, Whois and Google Safe Browsing Transparency Report, captured with Playwright/Chromium. DNS block attribution: compares the resolver under analysis with public reference resolvers (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1) using RCODE, the AA flag and RFC 8914 Extended DNS Errors (dig 9.11 and 9.18 formats). Attribution states: BLOQUEO_CONFIRMADO, BLOQUEO_PROBABLE, NO_ATRIBUIBLE, SIN_BLOQUEO, SIN_RESOLVER_ANALIZADO. Evidence package: HTML report, email-ready HTML, DOCX and ZIP with screenshots and raw dig output. Unit tests (unittest) for DNS parsing and attribution logic. Responsible use No credentials, no anti-bot bypass. Public sources are consulted under their terms of use; for high-volume analysis use the providers' official APIs. License: MIT

title: A Browser-Based Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Robust Phishing URL Detection
authors: Pratik Kumar Dungano; Deepak Kumar Verma; Chetankumar Chudasama; Om Prakash Suthar; Vipin Kr. Kushwaha
venue: CRC Press eBooks
abstract: Phishing attacks have become among the most influential cybercrimes at a very fast pace, taking advantage of technical vulnerabilities as well as human vulnerability. Current detection systems are usually unsuccessful with zero-day phishing links, maliciously designed links, and websites generated by AIs. In order to address these limitations, this paper suggests a new hybrid AI-based phishing detection system integrating the capabilities of deep learning, ensemble learning, anomaly detection, and explainable AI. We use a Convolutional Neural Network (CharCNN) which operates on a character level, a LightGBM that uses built lexical along with host-based features, as well as a Logistic Regression meta-classifier that combines the results of probabilistic models into one decision. To combat the severe drawback of zero-day resilience, we integrate an Isolation Forest anomaly detector that identifies unseen suspicious URLs, despite the use of classifiers which predict benign URLs. More so, we propose an uncertainty-aware prediction system that does not yield forced classification when the probabilities are uncertain, thus minimizing the number of false positives and false negatives. In order to increase user trust and the usability of the analyst, the framework has a explainability module which points out suspicious tokens (e.g., homoglyphs like g00gle.com or sensitive keywords like login-secure) directly in the browser. The entire system is implemented as a real-time browser extension which also allows to easily intercept and classify URLs with the minimum amount of latency. Evaluation on benchmark phishing datasets reveals that our model has an accuracy of 99.1, precision of 98.8 and recall of 99.3 as well as F1-score of 99.1 that is higher than base CNN, LightGBM, and BERT-based systems. As opposed to our previous work, our solution is the first to integrate zero-day anomaly detection, explainability, and uncertainty management into a practical, scalable, and deployable browser-based defence to enable the translation between academic research and practice in cybersecurity.

title: A Structured State Space Sequence Model for Multi-Class Classification of Malware
authors: Emmanuela Andam; Rana Shaaban; Emanuel Grant; Naima Kaabouch
abstract: By 2030, Internet of Things (IoT) devices are projected to reach 40 billion, with fast-paced technological advancements in fields such as industry, healthcare, agriculture, automobiles, and building/home automation systems. This expansion has created a large attack surface for cybercrime, as the majority of these devices open the door for cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities, as they lack adequate built-in security. Cybercriminals launch malware attacks to compromise systems or steal sensitive data, and once a system is compromised, a ransom is typically demanded for its release. Current cybersecurity measures in place are being outpaced by the rapid growth of the IoT, which is accompanied by a subsequent growth in malware variants being created per day. Recognizing this pitfall, this research examines and proposes a novel approach to malware detection and classification to safeguard devices from further attacks and make IoT systems more robust and secure. The framework proposed utilizes a Structured State Space Sequence (S4) model, which discretizes sequences of malware samples in a sequence and captures long-range dependencies, essentially identifying the "cause" and "effect" hidden within malware execution flow. This study presents two novel contributions: the first empirical application of the S4 model for malware analysis, and a comprehensive comparison of its performance against other deep learning architectures, laying the stepping stone for future research in this new paradigm.

title: Regulating the Crypto-Laundering Chain: A Comparative Study of Scam Compounds and Money Mule Mechanisms Within Criminal Networks
authors: Gioia Arnone
venue: Risks
abstract: This paper examines how scam compounds, money mules and crypto-assets operate as interdependent elements of contemporary money-laundering chains. It assesses whether existing anti-money laundering (AML) and crypto-asset regulatory frameworks are capable of disrupting these chains holistically, rather than addressing individual components in isolation, with particular reference to scam-compound activity in Southeast Asia. The study adopts a qualitative comparative case-study methodology grounded in legal and regulatory analysis. Four empirically grounded cases are examined: two Southeast Asian scam-compound enforcement cases (Cambodia and Myanmar) and two European crypto-asset seizure cases (Ireland and Italy). Judicial decisions, enforcement actions and regulatory instruments are analysed through a chain-based analytical framework aligned with Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards, the EU Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) and the Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) framework. The analysis reveals a structural divergence in enforcement strategies: Southeast Asian responses increasingly prioritise network- and infrastructure-level disruption of scam compounds, whereas European approaches remain largely centred on post-offence crypto-asset seizure through traditional proceeds-of-crime mechanisms. Across all jurisdictions, money mules emerge as a critical yet systematically under-regulated intermediary layer enabling the resilience of crypto-laundering operations. The paper advances existing AML typologies by conceptualising scam compounds, money mules and crypto-assets as interconnected components of a single crypto-laundering chain. This chain-based perspective offers a novel analytical and regulatory lens for understanding organised crypto-enabled fraud. The study is based on a qualitative, case-based design and does not aim for statistical generalisation. However, the analytical framework developed is transferable to other jurisdictions experiencing similar scam-compound and crypto-laundering dynamics. The findings suggest that effective AML enforcement requires coordinated intervention across multiple nodes of the laundering chain, including scam compound infrastructure and money mule networks, alongside traditional asset-seizure mechanisms and CASP supervision. By highlighting the structural links between scam compounds, coercive labour and crypto-laundering mechanisms, the paper underscores the broader social harms of crypto-enabled fraud and the need for integrated regulatory responses that address both financial crime and human exploitation.

title: Wavelet-Based and MAML-Driven Framework for Enhanced Few-Shot Malware Classification
authors: Abdullah Almuqrin; Ibrahim Mutambik; Majed Abusharhah
venue: Applied Sciences
abstract: Traditional malware classification approaches primarily address fixed sets of well-studied malware types and therefore struggle to accommodate the continual emergence of novel or previously unseen malware strains. While visualization-based strategies have shown promise in few-shot malware classification, existing methods often produce representations with limited semantic richness. In parallel, few-shot learning models frequently converge with suboptimal solutions, limiting their ability to generalize effectively to new classes. To address these challenges, we propose MetaWave, a unified framework that jointly optimizes both data representation and model learning for few-shot malware classification. Rather than treating feature representation and learning strategy as largely independent stages, MetaWave is formulated as an explicit representation–adaptation integration framework that combines multi-view malware encoding with meta-learning-based optimization. At the data level, we propose a Wavelet Transform-based Malware Representation method that leverages multi-scale frequency analysis and complementary views to generate semantically enriched representations. At the model level, we adopt Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) to optimize model initialization for rapid adaptation to unseen tasks under limited data conditions. Extensive experiments are conducted on two benchmark datasets, EMBER and Malicia, under a 5-way 5-shot protocol with disjoint class splits to ensure evaluation on previously unseen malware families. The proposed framework achieves superior performance, reaching 97.8% accuracy on EMBER and 96.2% on Malicia, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods. These results indicate that jointly enhancing representation quality and model adaptability can improve classification accuracy and unseen-family performance under the evaluated 5-way 5-shot protocol. Overall, MetaWave provides an effective framework for few-shot malware classification and offers a promising basis for detecting emerging malware under limited-data conditions, while robustness to adversarial perturbation, obfuscation, and polymorphism remains to be validated through dedicated future evaluation.
affiliations: King Saud University; Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University

title: Love Scam: Sejauh Manakah Undang-Undang melindungi Mangsa Love Scam di Malaysia?
authors: Siti Zalzaliza Zulkhafri; Nazura Abdul Manap; Ramalinggam Rajamanickam
venue: Jurnal Undang-Undang dan Masyarakat
abstract: Kemajuan teknologi seperti Internet dan media sosial memainkan peranan yang sangat penting dalam dunia teknologi maklumat kerana ia secara tidak langsung dapat membantu dalam menyediakan saluran komunikasi serta maklumat terkini kepada para pengguna di seluruh dunia. Di Malaysia, penggunaan teknologi, seperti telefon pintar dan komputer riba telah menyumbang kepada peningkatan penggunaan Internet dan media sosial dalam kalangan masyarakat. Walaupun terdapat kebaikan dari segi pembangunan teknologi maklumat selaras dengan arus permodenan zaman, namun, inovasi teknologi ini juga merupakan antara cabaran terbesar masyarakat. Hal ini dikatakan demikian kerana penggunaan teknologi, seperti Internet dan media sosial ini boleh membawa kemudaratan atau masalah kepada pengguna sama ada dari sudut sosial mahupun undang-undang. Antaranya, penggunaan teknologi dan media sosial telah menyumbang kepada gejala love scam (penipuan cinta siber) yang melibatkan golongan wanita, remaja dan juga golongan lain yang mudah terpengaruh. Perkembangan undang-undang perlu diukur untuk menilai sama ada undang-undang sedia ada dapat bertindak secara menyeluruh dalam melindungi mangsa penipuan cinta siber ini. Oleh hal yang demikian, artikel ini membincangkan takat undang-undang sedia ada dapat melindungi mangsa jenayah love scam ini dengan menilai sama ada undang-undang sedia ada sudah mencukupi untuk membanteras jenayah penipuan cinta siber ini daripada terus berleluasa. Walaupun terdapat undang-undang sedia ada di Malaysia, namun, jenayah love scam ini masih terus meningkat bilangannya. Perbandingan dengan negara lain, seperti Australia dan United Kingdom adalah penting untuk melihat sejauh manakah undang-undang di negara tersebut menangani isu love scam ini. Sesungguhnya, dapat disimpulkan bahawa walaupun ketiga-tiga buah negara mempunyai undang-undang yang mengawal selia jenayah love scam siber ini, namun, undang-undang sedia ada tersebut masih belum cukup untuk melindungi mangsa love scam siber secara menyeluruh. Kata kunci: Kemajuan teknologi; penipuan cinta; penipuan cinta siber; media sosial; undang-undang. Technological advancements such as the Internet and social media play a crucial role in the world of information technology as it indirectly help in providing communication channels and the latest information to users around the world. In Malaysia, the use of technology, such as smartphones and laptops has contributed to the increase in the use of the Internet and social media among the community. Although there are benefits in terms of development of information technology in line with current modernity, however, this technological innovation is also one of the society’s biggest challenges. This is because the use of technology, such as the Internet and social media, can bring harm or problems to users either from a social or legal standpoint. Among them, the use of technology and social media has contributed to issues of love scams (also known as cyber love scams) involving women, teenagers and other vulnerable groups. Legal developments need to be measured to assess whether existing laws can act comprehensively in protecting the victims of love scams. Therefore, this article discusses the extent to which current laws can protect the victims of love scams by assessing whether current laws are sufficient to combat love scams. Although there are existing laws in Malaysia, however, this love scam crime continues to increase in number. Comparison with other countries, such as Australia and the United Kingdom is important to see how far the laws in those countries deal with this love scam issue. Indeed, it can be concluded that although all three countries have laws that regulate this crime of love scams, however, there is still insufficent legal protection for the victims of love scams as a whole. Keywords: Technological advancements, love scams, cyber love scams, internet, social media, law.

title: Psychosocial and cultural dynamics shaping substance use and internet fraud among Nigerian youths
authors: Lateef Olutoyin Oluwole; Adetunji Obadeji; Adedotun Samuel Ajiboye; Mary Aanuoluwapo Atofarati
venue: Discover Mental Health
abstract: BACKGROUND: The rapid expansion of digital technologies has introduced new psychosocial risks for young people, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. In Nigeria, increasing rates of psychoactive substance use among youths have emerged alongside the growing prevalence of internet fraud ("Yahoo-Yahoo"), raising concerns about their interconnected social, psychological, and cultural drivers. AIMS: This study explored the relationship between psychoactive substance use and engagement in internet fraud among Nigerian youths, with particular attention to the social, economic, psychological, and cultural contexts shaping this association. METHOD: A qualitative design was employed using four focus group discussions with 22 young adults receiving treatment for substance-related mental and behavioural disorders at a tertiary health facility in southwestern Nigeria. Some participants reported direct or indirect involvement in internet fraud. Data were analyzed thematically using Braun and Clarke's framework. RESULTS: Findings revealed a complex, bidirectional relationship between substance use and internet fraud, mediated by peer influence, economic marginalization, moral normalization, and culturally embedded expectations of success. Psychoactive substances were perceived as facilitating emotional coping, confidence, and endurance during fraudulent activities, while proceeds from cyber fraud often sustained continued substance use. Despite varying degrees of social acceptance, participants reported guilt, psychological distress, and significant mental health risks. CONCLUSIONS: Psychoactive substance use and internet fraud among Nigerian youths appear less as isolated deviant behaviours and more as maladaptive coping strategies within contexts of structural inequality. There is an urgent need for integrated, youth-focused interventions that address mental health, family dynamics, and economic opportunities.
affiliations: Ekiti State University; Federal University Oye Ekiti

title: Memory and executive functioning show differential associations with scam susceptibility in middle to older adulthood
authors: Cassidy P. Molinare; Belinda Y Zhang; Mark E. Sanderson‐Cimino; Melanie Leguizamon; Emma Oyen; Daisy T Noriega-Makarskyy; Jenna Axelrod; Aaron C. Lim; Camdyn Wu; Maanya Agarwal; Laura A. Mosqueda; S. Duke Han
venue: medRxiv
abstract: Abstract Objectives The rising prevalence of financial exploitation among older adults has prompted research on the cognitive mechanisms underlying financial decision making in later life. Prior work has demonstrated a link between cognitive impairment and financial vulnerability. The present study examined the unique contributions of composite measures of memory and executive functioning to scam susceptibility in middle-aged to older adults without dementia. Methods One hundred and fifty-one participants (age= 68.2 ± 8.0 years, 72.2% female, years of education= 16.4 ± 2.2) completed standard neuropsychological measures from the Uniform Data Set (UDS), Version 3, and the California Verbal Learning Test, Second Edition, and a self-report scam susceptibility measure. Psychometrically robust composite scores, the UDS-M+ and UDS3-EF, were computed to represent memory and executive functioning domains. Linear regression models examined independent associations between UDS-M+ and UDS3-EF performance and scam susceptibility. Nested model comparisons evaluated unique contributions of the UDS-M+ and UDS3-EF when included in a joint model. Results Lower UDS-M+ (b= -0.25, 95% CI [-0.45, -0.04], p = .018) and lower UDS3-EF (b= - 0.33, 95% CI [-0.54, -0.12], p = .002) scores were independently associated with greater scam susceptibility after adjusting for age, sex, years of education, and income. However, only UDS3-EF remained significant in a joint model. Post hoc analyses revealed that only memory was associated with scam susceptibility in middle-aged adults whereas only executive functioning was significant in older adults. Conclusions These findings highlight the importance of monitoring memory and executive functioning across middle to older adulthood when considering susceptibility to scams. Statement of Research Significance Research Question(s) or Topic(s) This study evaluated the contributions of memory and executive functioning to scam susceptibility in middle-aged to older adults without dementia using cognitive composite scores and whether these associations differed across middle-aged and older adult groups. Main Findings After adjusting for age, sex, education, and income, memory (b= -0.25, 95% CI [-0.45, -0.04], p = .018) and executive functioning (b= -0.33, 95% CI [-0.54, -0.12], p = .002) each demonstrated an independent inverse association with scam susceptibility. In a joint model, only executive functioning was associated with scam susceptibility. When comparing age groups, only memory was significant in middle age while only executive functioning was significant in older adults. Study Contributions These results extend prior research by clarifying the unique contributions of memory and executive functioning to financial vulnerability and suggesting there may be differences in the cognitive processes used for financial decision making across stages of older adulthood.
affiliations: University of Southern California; Keck Hospital of USC

title: A Review of Phishing Detection Techniques Using Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing
authors: Sunita Dixit
venue: Journal of Global Research in Multidisciplinary Studies(JGRMS)
abstract: The goal of phishing attacks, which rank high among cyber risks, is to steal sensitive information (such as login passwords, financial data, and more) from unsuspecting people and companies. Blacklist, whitelist, rule, heuristic, and signature-based detection methods are no longer suitable due to the rising sophistication of phishing schemes. As a result, ML, DL, and NLP are rapidly becoming into effective instruments for detecting both well-known and brand-new forms of phishing. Background on phishing assaults, old ways of detecting them, and recent advances in intelligent phishing detection are all included in this article. It delves into several machine learning algorithms such as decision tree, LSTM, ANN, CNN, and RNN, as well as deep learning models like KNN, NB, and SVM. Also, natural language processing methods including word embedding, sentiment analysis, text categorization, and tokenization are explored with the aim of detecting phishing material. Presenting a comprehensive, precise, and up-to-the-minute phishing detection system is the ultimate goal of this study, which focuses on machine learning frameworks, performance indicators, present obstacles, and future research directions.
affiliations: St. Andrews Institute of Technology and Management

title: Prompt Injection Through Forensic Evidence: A Taxonomy and Proof of Concept of Anti-Forensic Attacks on LLM-Assisted Digital Investigations
authors: Frank Breitinger; Jan Gruber; Christopher Hargreaves; Jan-Niclas Hilgert; Gaëtan Michelet; Mark Scanlon
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are entering digital forensics as examination assistants and autonomous agents. Digital forensics inverts the usual setting for indirect prompt injection: the evidence under analysis is attacker-controlled by definition, and the examiner is obliged to read it closely. This makes the reasoning layer a new anti-forensic target, next to the classical ones of data and tools. Classical anti-forensic taxonomies do not cover it, and prompt injection defences do not anticipate it. We extend the anti-forensic model to reflect the manipulation of reasoning, and present a taxonomy of attacks carried through adversarial evidence: an attacker selects an objective, a technique, a payload location, and a concealment method. We observe a perception gap, i.e., the fact that deterministic tools, the human examiner, and the model perceive the same evidence differently, which is what lets an injection reach the model unseen by the examiner. We demonstrate three attacks against an LLM-assisted analysis pipeline, changing a reported conclusion, writing attacker-chosen content to the analyst's workstation, and causing outbound network traffic, each driven only by text planted on the seized device. Mitigations to these attacks are also proposed.
affiliations: University of Augsburg; Karlsruhe Institute of Technology; University of Oxford; Fraunhofer Institute for Communication, Information Processing and Ergonomics; University College Dublin

title: THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN INTERNET FRAUD AND PSYCHOACTIVE SUBSTANCE USE DISORDER: A NARRATIVE REVIEW
authors: J Falade; Oluwafemi Blessing Ajiboye; B. A. Eegunranti; Foluso Olamide Ojo
venue: FUDMA Journal of Sciences
abstract: Increase in internet fraud is a growing public health issue, particularly in relation to substance use disorders among youth and adolescents. Review explores the complex relationship between internet fraud and drug addiction, focusing on potential solutions to reduce addiction, particularly in young people. A comprehensive search was conducted between March and November 2023 across Google Scholar, PubMed, and the Cochrane Library to gather articles on internet fraud and drug addiction. The internet serves various roles, including cybercrime such as identity theft, online drug trafficking, and cyberstalking, which introduce unique risks. Addiction is influenced by neurobiological, psychological, and societal factors, with the brain's reward system, genetics, environment, and peer pressure playing key roles. The relationship between internet fraud and addiction is bidirectional, where each worsens the other. The review emphasizes the need to raise awareness about the interconnected risks of internet fraud and drug abuse, particularly for youth.

title: Pertanggungjawaban Pidana Perbankan Atas Kelalaian Terhadap Raibnya Dana Nasabah Akibat Phishing
authors: Priskila Kurniawati; Rena Sitanggang
venue: Public Service and Governance Journal
abstract: Perkembangan teknologi informasi telah meningkatkan penggunaan layanan perbankan digital dalam masyarakat. Kondisi tersebut diikuti dengan meningkatnya kejahatan siber, khususnya Phishing, yang menyebabkan hilangnya dana nasabah melalui manipulasi data dan penyalahgunaan sistem elektronik. Kejahatan Phishing tidak hanya menimbulkan kerugian bagi nasabah, tetapi juga menimbulkan persoalan hukum mengenai tanggung jawab perbankan terhadap keamanan sistem dan perlindungan dana nasabah. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis bentuk kelalaian perbankan dalam perlindungan sistem elektronik serta pertanggungjawaban pidana bank terhadap raibnya dana nasabah akibat Phishing. Penelitian menggunakan metode hukum normatif dengan pendekatan perundang-undangan dan pendekatan konseptual. Bahan hukum diperoleh melalui studi kepustakaan yang terdiri dari peraturan perundang-undangan, literatur hukum, jurnal ilmiah, dan dokumen terkait. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa kelalaian perbankan dapat dilihat dari lemahnya sistem keamanan digital, pengawasan transaksi elektronik, serta perlindungan data nasabah. Pertanggungjawaban pidana terhadap pihak perbankan dapat dikaitkan dengan prinsip corporate criminal liability apabila terbukti terdapat unsur kelalaian yang mengakibatkan kerugian nasabah. Pengaturan mengenai perlindungan konsumen, keamanan sistem elektronik, dan perlindungan data pribadi menjadi dasar penting dalam menentukan tanggung jawab hukum perbankan terhadap korban Phishing. Katakunci: Pertanggungjawaban Pidana, Perbankan, Phishing, Cybercrime, Perlindungan Nasabah.

title: Know the Normal, Track the Attack: Context-Grounded and Stateful LLM Investigation over System Provenance
authors: Lijie Zheng; Ji He; Ying Wang; Huang Zhang; Yulong Shen
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
abstract: Provenance-based intrusion detection systems (PIDSs) identify suspicious activity in audit streams, but their outputs remain difficult to turn into coherent attack narratives. Direct LLM analyses of local anomalous subgraphs lack deployment-specific normal-behavior knowledge and validated attack state across evidence fragments. This can cause unsupported attack interpretations of routine activities and incorrect attribution of temporally dispersed evidence to attack stages. We present ANCHOR, an investigation-oriented provenance system that combines evidence curation with context-grounded LLM reasoning. It calibrates anomaly judgments by relation type and links anomalous windows through rare relation-role patterns. The resulting evidence queues preserve causal structure, temporal boundaries, and cross-window continuity. The investigator interprets process-centered evidence using two complementary forms of context. Deployment Context combines environment-specific interaction and object baselines with high-risk security knowledge. Case Context uses a confidence-gated Attack-Tracking Cache to maintain investigation state across windows. Correlating current evidence with high-confidence prior findings, ANCHOR incrementally reconstructs attack narratives organized by kill-chain stages. We evaluate ANCHOR on six DARPA Transparent Computing E3/E5 datasets across three operating systems. Controlled evidence-level and end-to-end comparisons show improved overall IoC recovery and attack-stage attribution over state-of-the-art provenance-based baselines. These gains persist under a fixed LLM backbone in our evaluation. ANCHOR processes a full audit day at dollar-level API cost, supporting practical, context-grounded investigation across windows.

title: Forensic insights into mortality and challenges in post-mortem investigations of homeless individuals: a 10-year study (2014–2024) in Milan, Italy
authors: Stefano Tambuzzi; Devis Valleriani; Chiara Carsana; Paola Arzenati; Debora Mazzarelli; Cristina Cattaneo
venue: International Journal of Legal Medicine
abstract: Forensic medicine represents a critical socio-health observatory for socially marginalized populations. This study provides the first systematic retrospective forensic analysis of mortality among people experiencing homelessness in Italy. We examined 104 decedents undergoing autopsy in Milan between 2014 and 2024. The annual number of autopsied homeless decedents increased over the study period, peaking in 2023-2024. The majority of deaths occurred in indoor public spaces (45/104, 43.3%), with the remainder in hospitals or green areas, reflecting extreme social marginalization and environmental exposure. Anamnestic data were available for 56/104 cases (53.8%), of whom 42 (75%) had chronic medical conditions, while psychiatric or psychosocial histories were known for 43/104 cases (41.3%). These figures likely underestimate the true burden due to fragmented healthcare access and incomplete documentation. Causes of death were classified as natural (25/104, 24.0%), non-natural (17/104, 16.4%), or undetermined (62/104, 59.6%). Natural deaths, predominantly in middle-aged adults, illustrate accelerated health deterioration associated with homelessness, while non-natural deaths reflect heightened exposure to hazardous urban environments. Undetermined deaths - mainly acute circulatory insufficiency without macroscopic findings - highlight substantial gaps in post-mortem evaluation. Toxicological and histological analyses were rarely performed, revealing procedural and structural constraints that impede accurate cause-of-death determination in socially vulnerable and clinically complex populations. These findings uncover preventable and identifiable patterns of mortality, emphasize the forensic and public health value of comprehensive post-mortem investigation, and call for integrated strategies combining proactive healthcare delivery, harm reduction, and standardized forensic protocols to improve diagnostic accuracy and strengthen mortality surveillance in homeless populations.

title: MODEL OF RANSOMWARE SPREAD IN CORPORATE NETWORKS: THE IMPACT OF SEGMENTATION AND ZERO TRUST ON THE SPEED OF COMPROMISE
authors: O I Harasymchuk; Y.M.. Kasatkin
venue: Komp'ûternì sistemi ta merežì
abstract: The basis of the work is the study of the influence of corporate network architecture and internal security policies on the dynamics of ransomware spread, in particular, an assessment of the effectiveness of network segmentation and the Zero Trust concept as mechanisms for limiting lateral movement. To this end, a theoretical analysis of modern attacks was conducted and a simulation model of malware spread in a corporate network was developed. The network was formalized in the form of a graph, and the spread process was described using the SIR model. The implementation was performed in Python using the networkx library, which made it possible to conduct a series of experiments for different scenarios: a flat, segmented network, and a network with Zero Trust principles. The modeling results showed that in flat networks ransomware attacks are characterized by high speed and scale even with a single penetration. Segmentation significantly reduces the infection rate and localizes the attack within segments, while Zero Trust additionally limits the spread due to access control and node isolation. The results obtained confirm the decisive role of lateral movement and the feasibility of using architectural mechanisms for managing internal trust. The practical value lies in the possibility of using the model to analyze the effectiveness of architectural solutions in the field of cybersecurity and in the educational process of training information security specialists. Keywords: ransomware; corporate network; lateral movement; network segmentation; Zero Trust; propagation modeling; SIR model; cybersecurity, attack, malware, network node.

title: Regulatory Gaps and Protection Failures: A Socio-Legal Study of Fraud Cases Involving Indonesian Migrant Workers
authors: Sudarto M. Abukasim; Sutarsa Sutarsa; Dwi Slamet Raharjo; Akbar Nur Salim; Wasino Wasino; Mustafa Mustafa
venue: Journal of Creative Power and Ambition
abstract: International labor migration has become one of the most significant global phenomena in the era of modern globalization. This study aims to analyze the regulatory gap and weak legal protection for Indonesian migrant workers (PMI) in cases of fraud and exploitation of migrant workers. The research uses a socio-legal approach, employing normative analysis of laws and regulations, as well as empirical studies based on court decisions, BP2MI reports, online media, and investigative documents from PMI cases for the 2020–2025 period. Thematic analysis was used to identify patterns of fraud, institutional weaknesses, and socio-legal factors that affect the effectiveness of migrant worker protections. The results of the study show that although Indonesia already has a legal framework through Law Number 18 of 2017 concerning the Protection of Indonesian Migrant Workers, the practice of illegal recruitment and exploitation is still taking place systematically. Forms of fraud include document forgery, use of non-procedural visas, fake employment contracts, wage deductions, passport confiscation, and digital fraud through social media. The study found gaps between formal regulation and implementation, particularly in recruitment supervision, administrative verification, inter-agency coordination, and victim recovery mechanisms. In addition, poverty, low education, lack of legal literacy, and limited employment also increase the vulnerability of migrant workers. Therefore, reform of migrant worker protection is needed by strengthening supervision, institutional reform, digitizing the migration system, and international cooperation.

title: Federated ConvNeXt-swin temporal fusion network for malware and botnet detection in IoT systems
authors: Faisal S. Alsubaei; Abdulwahab Ali Almazroi; Nasir Ayub
venue: Scientific Reports
abstract: The rapid expansion of Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructures has significantly increased the exposure of edge devices to malware and botnet attacks. Conventional intrusion detection systems are largely centralized and struggle to operate effectively in decentralized, heterogeneous, and privacy-sensitive IoT environments, thereby limiting scalability and robustness. To address these challenges, this study proposes the Federated ConvNeXt-Swin Temporal Fusion Network (F-CSTFNet), a federated deep learning framework designed for distributed IoT malware and botnet detection. The proposed architecture integrates ConvNeXt-based convolutional feature extraction with Swin Transformer temporal attention to capture both local traffic patterns and long-range behavioral dependencies within network flows. This hybrid convolution-attention design enables the detection of short-term anomalies as well as evolving attack dynamics directly from network telemetry. In addition, a channel-adaptive feature recalibration mechanism enhances robustness when learning from heterogeneous and noisy client data. The model is trained using a federated learning paradigm that enables multiple IoT clients to collaboratively learn a global model without sharing raw data, thereby preserving data privacy and locality. Extensive experiments conducted on the IoT-23 and N-BaIoT datasets demonstrate that F-CSTFNet outperforms several state-of-the-art centralized and federated baselines in terms of detection accuracy, convergence stability, and client-level fairness. The framework also achieves low performance variance across clients, a high Jain's Fairness Index (JFI), and reduced inequality during distributed training. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed architecture as a scalable, privacy-preserving, and resilient intrusion detection framework for next-generation IoT security systems.

title: Legal regulation and liability for online fraud based on the use of deepfake technologies and social engineering: foreign experience and directions for its adoption
authors: A.B. Saktaganova; Индира Сактаганова
venue: Bulletin of the Karaganda University “Law Series”
abstract: In the context of the rapid development of digital technologies, online fraud based on the use of deepfake technologies and social engineering methods poses a significant threat to public safety. The aim of this study is to analyse the legal regulation and liability measures for such crimes in foreign countries, as well as to identify areas where positive international experience can be used to improve national legislation. The study employs general scientific and special methods of cognition, including analysis, synthesis, induction and deduction, as well as formal-legal, comparative-legal and systemic-structural methods. The work examines normative legal acts, judicial practice and doctrinal approaches in a number of foreign countries, including the European Union, the United States and Asian countries, regulating liability for digital forms of fraud. As a result, the main models of legal response to crimes involving deepfakes and social engineering were identified, and their strengths and weaknesses were established. The study concludes that a comprehensive approach to legal regulation is necessary, including clarifying the elements of offences, strengthening preventive measures, and developing international cooperation. The results obtained can be used to formulate proposals for improving criminal and information legislation.
affiliations: L. N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University

title: A CNN–BiLSTM Hybrid Model for Email Phishing Detection
authors: Nicholas Muriuki
venue: Journal of Intelligent Systems and Applied Data Science
abstract: Email phishing is by far one of the most common and harmful cybersecurity risks that make use of misguided communication methods to breach sensitive user data. Phishing attacks keep changing, which greatly constrains the performance of conventional rule-based and classical machine-learning methods of detection. The proposed study will introduce a hybrid deep learning model that combines Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Bidirectional Long Short-term Memory (Bi-LSTM) networks to detect emails with high phishing accuracy. The model proposed examines various elements of email, such as, email headers, subject lines, message bodies and embedded URLs, in the form of a rich feature representation that represents structural and contextual features. The datasets collected in the real world, PhishTank and Mendeley repositories, were preprocessed by feature binning, redundancy reduction as well as class balancing to improve the quality of data and generalization. The experimental findings indicate that CNNBILSTM model has a high accuracy (96), precision (95.9), recall (96) and ROC-AUC (0.99), which is better than a number of baseline models, including Support Vector Machines (SVM), Decision Trees, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and individual neural networks. The statistical analysis also verifies that the performance improvements are substantial (p < 0.05) and the confidence intervals are not wide which means the study is very consistent and reliable. Based on the findings, it is possible to note that the CNN-BiLSTM model represents a reliable, scalable, and high-performance solution that can be applied to real-time email phishing detection in the contemporary cybersecurity settings.

title: Moral Boundary Work and the Recasting of Fraud as Hustle in Southwestern Nigeria
authors: Dare Adegoriolu
venue: Deviant Behavior
abstract: This article examines how self-identified fraudsters in Abeokuta reinterpret the Yoruba adage “ole lo ba omo je” to legitimize cyber fraud as. Drawing on 25 semi-structured interviews , it analyzes how respondents engage in moral boundary work by selectively redefining theft, labor, and legitimacy within youth precarity and distrust. It reveals that neutralization strategies reposition fraud as morally defensible relative to elite corruption. Furthermore, they reframed fraud as skilled labor requiring entrepreneurial competence. These discursive practices reflect an ongoing restructuring of moral categories in youth culture. Hence, foregrounding cultural reinterpretation of moral language positions the study among cybercrime scholarship in contemporary Africa.
affiliations: Ekiti State University; Adekunle Ajasin University; Obafemi Awolowo University

title: Deepfake Enabled Financial Fraud and Consumer Trust in Digital Finance: Can Vulnerability–Trust–Resilience Framework Be Applied in the United States of America?
authors: Simeon Gbimoiye Nenbee; ISRAEL TEGA GOLLEY; Ifeanyi Sunday (Ph.D.) Mgbataogu
venue: Journal of Economics Finance and Management Studies
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has made convincing synthetic identities, voices, images, and video cheaper and easier to produce. Financial institutions now face attacks directed not only at technical authentication, but also at the social cues through which customers and employees decide whom to trust. This study combines descriptive analysis of public United States fraud statistics with directed qualitative content analysis of 18 (eighteen) authoritative regulatory, law-enforcement, standards, and policy documents published between 2019 and 2025. Eight response mechanisms were coded: accountable ownership, identity verification, deepfake detection and provenance, transaction monitoring, human authentication and escalation, customer information, incident response and information sharing, and third-party governance. Incident response appeared in about 94% of the corpus while identity verification stood at 89%. Human authentication and transaction monitoring were present in 83% and 72%, respectively. Half of the documents addressed provenance or deepfake detection, whereas only 39% connected counter-fraud controls with customer communication. Public loss data confirm a rapidly worsening fraud environment but do not identify losses caused specifically by deepfakes, producing an attribution-denominator problem. The proposed Vulnerability–Trust–Resilience (VTR) framework shows how synthetic media can turn weaknesses in authentication and judgment into financial loss and wider distrust. Resilience therefore depends on layered verification, transaction-context controls, empowered human escalation, rapid recovery, and carefully calibrated communication—not on a single detector. It is therefore recommend that there is need to urgently develop testable propositions, a managerial scorecard, and a reproducible engagement agenda by the government to forestall the growing incidence of deekfake enabled financial fraud in the financial sector of the economy.

title: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning Techniques for Cross-Sector Fraud Detection in the South African Financial and Telecommunications Sectors
authors: Lufungula Osembe; Mukosi Lucky Mashudu
venue: International Journal of Business Ecosystem and Strategy (2687-2293)
abstract: Cross-sector fraud between South Africa’s financial and telecommunications sectors has intensified, driven by sophisticated criminal networks that exploit operational disparities between these industries. Traditional fraud detection systems, which depend on centralised data sharing and siloed organisational structures, encounter substantial legal and practical obstacles under the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA). These include restrictions on cross-entity data transfer, data minimisation requirements, and transparency obligations for automated decision-making. This study developed and evaluated a privacy-preserving framework that integrates Federated Learning (FL) and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to enable collaborative fraud detection while safeguarding customer privacy and ensuring regulatory compliance. A mixed-method approach was employed. Quantitative experiments were conducted on a dataset of 35,675 credit card transactions linked to telecommunications parameters, training a federated global model across simulated financial and telecommunications providers. A qualitative systematic literature review identified key barriers to cross-sector collaboration and distilled lessons from prior Federated Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence implementations. The federated model demonstrated strong detection performance, achieving a ROC-AUC of 0.98, near-perfect precision and recall for legitimate transactions, and an F1-score of 0.89 for the minority fraud class, all without exchanging raw customer data between institutions. SHAP analysis identified TransactionAmt and card1 as the most influential features, thereby satisfying POPIA's transparency mandates. While federated approaches did not consistently surpass siloed models in raw accuracy, this marginal trade-off reflects the essential privacy-utility equilibrium required for legal compliance. The framework effectively reconciled collective security with individual privacy, confirming that POPIA adherence need not diminish detection efficacy. This study provides a validated blueprint for financial and telecommunications providers in South Africa to collaboratively counter cross-sector fraud within regulatory constraints. The framework further supports audit trail generation and decision rationales, addressing compliance obligations. Drawing on systematic literature review insights, particularly regarding collaboration barriers and prior Federated Learning and Explainable Artificial Intelligence implementations, the findings offer regulators and investors practical guidance for meeting statutory requirements without compromising privacy rights.

title: Development of a Machine Learning-Based Model for Phishing Attack Detection in Smart-Home Environments
authors: Ayobami Olusesi; Olwabukunmi Onasanya; Oyinkansola Deji-Agboola; Ayo Isaac; Raphael Abolade
venue: FUDMA Journal of Sciences
abstract: Internet of Things (IoT)-powered smart home solutions are increasingly prevalent. As a result, they are significantly altering how we live today. Due to device heterogeneity, resource constraints, user awareness, and other factors, the systems that connect the Internet of Things (IoT) are themselves connected to other devices, making phishing attacks one of the most significant hazards in smart homes. Phishing undermines the privacy, security, and integrity of smart ecosystems by exploiting a user's trust through phony emails, voice squatting, URLs, among others. Since the current security techniques are insufficient, this study aim is to create a new tool based on machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques to check and detect phishing attacks on smart home systems. This study makes use of enron dataset from Kaggle which contains a total of 33,715 email samples. Data pre-processing was carried out to extract relevant features and attributes from the dataset. The phishector.py script provides a command line interface for processing emails and obtaining predictions. The model was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and FI-score as performance metrics. From the obtained results, bagged decision tree model shows a 99.94% accuracy, precision 99.8%, F1-score, 99.94%, and recall, 100% while Adobos a 97.98% accuracy, precision 96.23%, F1-score, 98.08%, and recall, 100%. The study's result has further demonstrated how the suggested methods can be applied to detect phishing assaults in smart homes and shield linked smart devices from cyberattacks.

title: An Intelligent Cybersecurity System for Phishing Attack Detection Using Machine Learning
authors: Raghupathi Hima Bindu
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
abstract: As our online presence grows, from online chats to online transactions and information sharing, phishing has turned out to be a significant concern in the world of cybersecurity. The term "phishing" describes a technique where hackers try to trick people into visiting fake websites and then persuade them to reveal their important information, like passwords or bank account numbers. The traditional "blacklist-based" technique, where a website's URL is checked against a list of known phishing websites, may not always be efficient in detecting new phishing websites. This project focuses on designing a machine learning-based phishing website detector that helps identify suspicious websites based on URL-based features. The machine learning algorithm will be trained on a dataset that consists of both phishing and legitimate websites. The features, such as URL length, domain name, presence of special characters, and security features, are extracted from the URLs and then used for classification. A simple web application, developed using the Flask web development library, can be used for this purpose. The results demonstrate that our system provides high accuracy with few false alarms. The approach is simple and flexible and can be easily incorporated into various cybersecurity tools in the real world. In summary, the approach is reliable and provides a solution for detecting phishing sites in the modern web environment.

title: Bridging The Enforcement Gap: Institutional Capacity and Judicial Interpretation in Tanzania’s Cybercrime Framework
authors: Engelberth Boniface
venue: East African Journal of Law and Ethics
abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies has significantly transformed social, economic, and governance systems worldwide, while simultaneously creating new opportunities for cybercrime. In Tanzania, the enactment of the Cybercrimes Act marked a critical step towards addressing cyber-related offences. However, despite the existence of a formal legal framework, cybercrime enforcement remains fraught with significant challenges. This article examines the gap between the normative legal framework and the practical realities of cybercrime enforcement in Tanzania, focusing specifically on institutional capacity and judicial interpretation. It argues that while the legal framework is relatively comprehensive, enforcement is undermined by limited technical capacity among enforcement agencies, inadequate digital forensic infrastructure, and inconsistencies in judicial interpretation of cybercrime laws. Adopting a doctrinal and comparative methodology, the article analyses Tanzania’s legal and institutional framework alongside selected jurisdictions to identify best practices and areas for reform. The findings indicate that effective cybercrime enforcement requires not only robust legislation but also well-equipped institutions and a judiciary capable of interpreting complex digital evidence and statutory provisions coherently. The article concludes by proposing targeted reforms aimed at strengthening institutional capacity, enhancing judicial competence, and promoting a more consistent and effective enforcement framework. These reforms are essential for bridging the enforcement gap and ensuring accountability in the digital age.

title: A comparative analysis of threat models in the context of cyber threat attribution
authors: Viktor Szulcsányi; Sándor Magyar
venue: International Journal of Information Security
abstract: Abstract The role of cyberspace in geopolitical conflicts, as the experience of recent decades clearly demonstrates, is continually expanding. The activities of state sponsored and other cyber actors are becoming increasingly frequent, complex, and sophisticated. To understand and analyze a potential cyber attack in detail, it is essential to identify and select an appropriate analytical framework. There are currently several frameworks and models for analyzing cyber threats, but these were developed for different purposes and primarily focus on technical analysis. However, when analyzing a complex attack, we must also consider additional non-technical aspects that are not or are only partially covered by the known models. This study evaluates the applicability of individual frameworks during cyber threat attribution based on a uniquely created set of criteria. The purpose of the comparative analysis is to understand the strengths, weaknesses, and shortcomings of individual models in light of the identification of cyber actors behind cyber threats. This study makes several contributions to the field of cyber threat attribution. First, it provides a comparative analysis of widely used threat models and demonstrates that none of them fully and sufficiently support attribution across all required analytical dimensions. Second, the paper introduces the HexAttribution Model, a novel multidimensional attribution framework that integrates technical, behavioral, motivational, and geopolitical factors within a single structure. Third, the study incorporates a structured reliability component that aggregates domain-level evidence through structural strength factors and scenario-specific weighting, making the assumptions behind attribution reasoning more explicit and reviewable. Finally, the paper presents a proof-of-concept demonstration, illustrating how the model can be applied in practice to support transparent and defensible attribution assessments.

title: E-HUNF: Explainable Hybrid Unsupervised Network Forensics for robust cybercrime anomaly detection
authors: A. Sangeetha; J. James Alaguraja; Rohaya Latip
venue: International Journal of Electronics and Telecommunications
abstract: Anomaly-based network forensics is very importantfor finding new types of cybercrime that don’t have reliablesignatures or labelled training data. But most unsuperviseddetectors only look at one view of normality and don’t giveany forensic interpretability. This study talks about E-HUNF,an Explainable Hybrid Unsupervised Framework that can findcrimes in network traffic. E-HUNF uses a manifold-aware, centreregularizedauto encoder to get compact latent representationsof flows. It then uses these to get three different anomaly scoresbased on reconstruction error, latent density, and distance from alearnt normalcy centre. These scores are combined into a hybridanomaly score with adaptive, percentile-based thresholding tohelp people make judgements that are mindful of risk. Anexplainability layer blends local linear surrogates with prototyperetrieval to show how each alert’s features and historical examplesare related. When tested on a standard network-forensicsdataset with benign, DoS, Probe/Scan, R2L/U2R, and Botnettraffic, E-HUNF got an accuracy of 0.987, an F1-Score of 0.978,a ROC-AUC of 0.995, and a PR-AUC of 0.993. It did betterthan Deep SVDD, DAGMM, VAE-AD, and Isolation Forest. Evenfor small R2L/U2R attacks, the class-wise F1-Scores stay above0.937. Ablation results show that adding density and boundarycues to reconstruction improves the F1 score by 3.3% overreconstruction-only versions. These results show that E-HUNFhas the best detection performance and the most useful forensictransparency for modern cyber-defence operations.

title: Typical investigative situations in the pre-trial investigation of cybercrimes
authors: I. S. Feshchenko
venue: Analytical and Comparative Jurisprudence
abstract: The article provides a comprehensive analysis of the essence, significance, and classification of typical investigative situations in the process of pre-trial investigation of cybercrimes. It is proven that typical investigative situations acquire particular importance at the initial stage of cybercrime investigation. It is revealed that the formation of an investigative situation is determined by a combination of objective and subjective factors, including the method of committing the crime, the conditions of emergence and destruction of digital traces, the behavior of participants in criminal proceedings, and the scope of available information. Scientific approaches to defining the concept of a “typical investigative situation” are analyzed, as a result of which its multifaceted nature is established. The generalization of scientific positions made it possible to conclude that a typical investigative situation includes not only information about the circumstances of the crime but also characteristics of the investigation process itself. The article classifies typical investigative situations according to various criteria. It is proven that the most favorable situation is voluntary confession; however, it is relatively rare in practice. Particular attention is paid to the classification of situations depending on the establishment of the method of committing the crime and the identity of the offender. Four basic models are identified, each determining the specifics of further investigative actions. Typical situations of the subsequent stage of investigation after notification of suspicion are also analyzed and divided into favorable and conflict situations. It is established that the effectiveness of investigation in conflict situations largely depends on the tactical skills of the investigator, particularly during interrogation. In addition, the article examines typical investigative situations of the final stage of pre-trial investigation, including the closure of criminal proceedings, exemption from criminal liability, or referral of the indictment to court. It is generalized that typical investigative situations serve as an effective tool for organizing the investigation, ensuring consistency, validity, and efficiency of the investigator’s activities under conditions of uncertainty characteristic of cybercrime.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Criminal Responsibility: Reconstructing Mens Rea and Attribution for AI-Assisted Cybercrime in Pakistan
authors: Syed Mudassir Shah
venue: Journal of Law & Social Studies
abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the scale, speed, personalization, and technical complexity of cybercrime without eliminating the need to attribute criminal responsibility to human actors. In Pakistan, the principal substantive framework remains the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act 2016, as amended in 2025, supplemented by the Pakistan Penal Code, the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order 1984, the Electronic Transactions Ordinance 2002, and the National Forensics Agency Act 2024. These laws are largely technology-neutral, yet AI-assisted offending creates evidential and conceptual pressure on traditional categories of intention, knowledge, authorization, causation, participation, and digital attribution. A person may use a generative model to draft phishing messages, automate reconnaissance, generate malicious code, create deepfakes, or optimize fraud while delegating numerous operational choices to software. The central legal problem is therefore not whether an AI system itself possesses criminal mens rea, but how courts should infer the mental state and causal contribution of programmers, operators, deployers, account holders, collaborators, and beneficiaries when machine output intervenes between human instruction and prohibited result. This paper argues against premature recognition of AI as a criminal subject. Current systems lack the normative agency, legal status, and punishment-sensitive interests that make criminal blame meaningful. Pakistani law should instead adopt a human-centred attribution framework built around purposeful use, knowledge of capabilities, control over deployment, foreseeability of system behaviour, acceptance of risk, contribution to the offence, and corroborated digital evidence. The paper proposes a four-layer attribution model covering identity, control, mental state, and causal contribution, together with evidential safeguards for logs, prompts, model outputs, account records, device forensics, and chain of custody. Reform should clarify AI-assisted liability without creating strict criminal responsibility for developers or users merely because an unpredictable model produced harmful output.

title: Cyber Threat Detection and Forensics for Ethereum Cryptocurrency Transactions
authors: Bhairab Sarma; Anupam Dutta; Prazna Lahkar; Chayanika Sarmah; Sangita Das
venue: Indian Journal Of Science And Technology
abstract: Objectives: To detect suspicious fraudulent activities in Ethereum wallet transactions using a graph-based machine learning and anomaly detection techniques. Method: From the Ethereum transaction graph, graph structure signals, timing cues, and node level attributes, have been analyzed using unsupervised models like Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor, and One-Class SVM to flag irregular wallet patterns. Finally, based on the transaction tracing pattern, illicit transactions are figure out for forensics actions. Findings: This work successfully found some suspicious Ethereum wallet behaviors by mixing graph analytics with unsupervised anomaly detection techniques. Graph-based signals such as PageRank, clustering coefficient, transaction frequency and entropy, boosted the capture of strange transaction behaviors that point out as suspicious operation. Isolation Forest did well at isolating the most extreme outliers, while LOF and One-Class SVM highlighted wallets with odd local density, plus a clear behavioral mismatch observed. Overall, the framework worked with the Ethereum transaction dataset from Kaggle, where wallet addresses. Out of 4000 transaction history, top 20 are figure out as may be fraudulent transaction based on their behaviors. Novelty: The study integrates graph analytics, blockchain forensics, and unsupervised machine learning to detect anomalous Ethereum wallet behavior without requiring labeled cryptocurrency fraud datasets. Here, only 0.5 percent Ethereum transaction are categorized as suspicious on this study. Keywords: Blockchain Tracing, Cryptocurrency Transactions, Ethereum, Fraud Detection, Graph Neural Network (GNN)

title: Practical Challenges in the Investigation and Prosecution of Cross-Border Cybercrime in Tanzania: A Doctrinal and Comparative Analysis
authors: Clara Charwe
venue: East African Journal of Law and Ethics
abstract: Tanzania’s Cybercrimes Act, 2015 confers on domestic courts jurisdiction over offences committed wholly or partly within the country, and over conduct directed against a computer system, device, data or person located in Tanzania, regardless of the offender’s nationality or location. Yet this statutory reach has not translated into effective enforcement when the offender, evidence, or infrastructure lies abroad. Using a doctrinal legal method with an integrated comparative element, this article examines the adequacy of Tanzania’s legal framework governing the investigation and prosecution of cross-border cybercrime, identifies the practical challenges that impede its enforcement, and proposes actionable reforms. It analyses the Cybercrimes Act, the Electronic Transactions Act, the Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters Act, and the Extradition Act against five theoretical lenses: territoriality, effects-based jurisdiction, international cooperation theory, Lessig’s regulatory theory, and Castells’ network theory, and compares Tanzania’s position with Kenya’s Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, 2018 and Rwanda’s Law No. 60/2018. The article finds that Tanzania’s jurisdictional trigger is already comparable to, or broader than, both comparators, so that the principal deficiency lies not in the assertion of jurisdiction but in the absence of a plainly worded effects test, in slow and generalist mutual legal assistance procedures unsuited to volatile digital evidence, in unresolved uncertainty over the cross-border chain of custody, and in Tanzania’s continued non-participation in the Budapest Convention and its Second Additional Protocol. The article recommends amending section 30 of the Cybercrimes Act to adopt an explicit effects-based clause modelled on Rwanda’s example, embedding an expedited, dedicated international-cooperation channel within the Cybercrimes Act itself along the lines of Kenya’s model, developing comprehensive cross-border digital evidence rules, and strengthening forensic capacity, institutional coordination and treaty participation.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Tanzania’s Cybercrimes Act in Preventing, Detecting and Prosecuting Mobile Money Fraud Through Unsolicited Messaging
authors: Dickson Mutabazi
venue: East African Journal of Law and Ethics
abstract: This article evaluates how far Tanzania’s Cybercrimes Act prevents, detects, and secures the prosecution of mobile money fraud that begins with an unsolicited message. It combines a doctrinal reading of sections 12 and 20 of the Act and its investigative provisions with empirical data collected in Dodoma through semi-structured interviews and open-ended questionnaires administered to twenty respondents from law enforcement, regulatory bodies, telecommunications companies, Parliament, academia and victims of fraud. The Act gives investigators a usable legal foundation, yet 65 per cent of respondents rated it less than effective. Section 12 is built around the manipulation of computer data or systems and fits awkwardly with schemes in which the victim is persuaded to make the transfer personally, while section 20 predates AI-generated voice calls, deepfakes, QR code scams and spoofed sender names, none of which the Act mentions. Enforcement is further weakened by thin forensic capacity, slow information sharing between agencies and service providers, and low digital literacy among users; no reported decision applying either provision to this kind of fraud could be found. The article argues that the problem is one of design as well as enforcement: an offence built around the manipulation of machines cannot be relied upon to punish the manipulation of people. It offers what appears to be the first focused legal assessment of this fraud vector in Tanzania and proposes legislative, institutional, and awareness-based reforms, including a technology-neutral offence of causing loss by electronic deception, mandatory fraud reporting by operators, a victim compensation mechanism that does not depend on conviction, stronger forensic capacity and sustained public education

title: FINANCIAL CYBER CRIME IN THE EMERGING WEB3 ECOSYSTEM: EVALUATING THE ADEQUACY OF INDIA'S CYBER LAW FRAMEWORK
authors: Meera PM
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Web3 technologies have evolved the structure of financial crimes. Financial cybercrime is now taking the shape of a category of crimes based on disintermediation, pseudonymity and cross-border movement with the support of cryptocurrencies, non-custodial wallets, decentralised exchanges, smart contracts, non-fungible tokens, and decentralised autonomous organisations. “This paper seeks to answer this question in respect of the Indian Cyber law. It looks at the Information Technology Act 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 and Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 and questions if they are sufficient to prevent, investigate, prosecute and remedy financial crime committed using Web3. It has taken a doctrinal approach, with comparisons drawn to the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation of the European Union and Payment Services Act of Singapore, and drawn on the guidelines of the Financial Action Task Force. The relevant Web3 crimes are aligned to the existing legislation to see the extent of existing law's reach, such as wallet compromising, phishing, rug pulls, smart contract exploits, ransomware, and layered money laundering. A combination of technology agnostic offences and a perimeter not yet defined for AML make India's framework workable with several legal gaps yet to be addressed. No legislation exists today explicitly related to virtual assets, and the jurisdiction and legal responsibility are not well defined. Laws are also not explicit about the existence of decentralised and autonomous code-based actors. Further, international cooperation and legal frameworks for the tracing and recovery of digital assets are still underdeveloped, which makes it difficult to do. These gaps have a real-time sense of urgency because the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal data indicate that the financial fraud losses reported have increased significantly in 2022–2024. The paper conclude that India’s current legal framework can respond to harm after it occurs, but it does not yet fully regulate the virtual asset ecosystem that can create such risks. This paper therefore suggests introducing a dedicated law for virtual digital assets, strengthening specialised agencies to investigate cyber-financial crimes, improving international cooperation in line with FATF Recommendation 15, and learning from the regulatory approaches followed by the European Union and Singapore.

title: Legal Deficiencies in Regulating Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity under the Information Technology Act, 2000: Addressing Phishing Escalation in 2024-2025
authors: Shambhavi Mishra; Nirmit Singh Chaudhry
venue: International Journal of Science Strategic Management and Technology
abstract: The inexorable integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with cybersecurity infractions has laid bare profound lacunae in the regulatory edifice enshrined under the Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act)[1]. This dissertation undertakes a doctrinal and empirical scrutiny of the legislative inadequacies in circumscribing AI-enabled cybersecurity menaces, with particular emphasis on the aggravated incidence of phishing contraventions during the period 2024-2025. Phishing, metamorphosed through AI instrumentalities such as deepfake artefacts, generative adversarial networks, and algorithmic social engineering, evinces a dissonance with the IT Act's antiquated provisions, inter alia Sections 43, 66, 66D, and the now-expunged Section 66A. Predicated upon CERT-In advisories and National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB)[2] compendia documenting a 150% augmentation in phishing cognizances from 2023 to 2025, the inquiry elucidates the paucity of AI-tailored nomenclatures, vicarious liability paradigms for AI progenitors, and compulsive ethical probity audits, thereby vitiating prosecutorial efficacy. A cardinal infirmity resides in the IT Act's techno-agnostic conspectus, antecedent to contemporaneous AI architectures encompassing machine learning and vast parametric reservoirs. Section 43A, mandating "reasonable security practices" for sensitive personal data, proscribes perspicuity vis-à-vis AI-orchestrated phishing, exemplified by phoneme-cloned impostures or hyper-granular assaults leveraging exfiltrated sociometric intelligence. The 2024-2025 phishing efflorescence manifest in emblematic precedents like AI-abetted impostures upon UPSC supplicants and pecuniary institutions (vide RBI circulars) bespeaks adjudicative impediments: retarded CERT-In intimation pursuant to Section 70B, attenuated intermediary safe harbours under Section 79, and the absenation of preemptive AI peril valuations. Juxtaposed against supranational precedents, including the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act, 2024[3] (classificatory high-risk impositions) and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, India's retardance is accentuated, notwithstanding the Digital

title: Innovations in Cardless Artificial Intelligence Banking: A Comprehensive Framework for Cyber Secure and Fraud Mitigation using Machine Learning Algorithms
authors: Md Israfeel
venue: ArXiv.org
abstract: The advent of cardless artificial intelligence (AI) banking heralds a paradigm shift in the financial landscape, offering users unprecedented security and convenience. This paper outlines a comprehensive framework designed to enhance cybersecurity, introduce auto-generated virtual cards, and mitigate fraud risks within cardless AI banking systems. The framework envisions a future banking architecture that employs AI-powered data cryptography to create secure virtual cards for seamless transactions. By emphasizing secure communication channels, it ensures the integrity of financial activities among banking systems, cardholders, and third-party vendors. AI-based authorization methodologies play a pivotal role in authenticating each transaction while proactively identifying potential fraud, demonstrating the framework's efficacy in fortifying cardless AI banking security. The initial approach, featuring an AI-driven, feature-based banking system, ensures the generation of virtual cards with encrypted data, minimizing information exposure and reducing fraud risks. Integrating a machine learning algorithm adds an additional layer of protection against potential fraudulent activities. In conclusion, the proposed framework establishes a holistic cybersecurity and fraud-mitigation paradigm for cardless AI banking systems. Its implementation empowers financial institutions to address security concerns associated with traditional banking, paving the way for a future banking landscape that is not only fraud-resistant but also secure and convenient for users.

title: Social Engineering Before Cybersecurity
authors: Daniel Rosehill; Gemini 3.1 (Flash); Chatterbox TTS
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Episode summary: Most people think social engineering started with cybersecurity. But the practice of manipulating people to gain access or information is as old as civilization itself. In this episode, we trace the actual lineage — from the Trojan Horse to the Cambridge Five spy ring, from Renaissance con artists to the CIA's Simple Sabotage Field Manual. We break down the core psychological vulnerabilities (authority, urgency, social proof) and the techniques (pretexting, baiting, tailgating) that predate digital technology by centuries. If you think social engineering is just phishing emails, this history will change how you see human nature as an attack surface. Show Notes Social engineering is widely associated with Kevin Mitnick and cybersecurity, but the discipline predates both by centuries. This episode traces the actual history — starting with the term itself, which was coined by a Dutch industrialist in the late 19th century to describe scientific management of human relations, not deception. The modern security meaning emerged through phone phreaking in the 1980s and 90s, but the practice is ancient. Examples from Herodotus and the Trojan Horse show that pretexting, emotional appeals, and physical props were used in antiquity. Renaissance con artists like Count Cagliostro exploited authority and deference reflexes. The Cambridge Five spy ring infiltrated British intelligence through class-based trust — not hacking, but relationship cultivation over years. The CIA's Office of Technical Service studied behavioral science, including the MICE framework (Money, Ideology, Coercion, Ego) for recruitment, and the Simple Sabotage Field Manual taught bureaucratic friction as a weapon. The episode maps a framework: psychological vulnerabilities (authority, urgency, social proof, scarcity, liking, fear) are the attack surface of human cognition. Techniques like pretexting, baiting, tailgating, quid pro quo, and phishing are simply ways to trigger those vulnerabilities. The honey trap, kompromat, and romance scams all share the same underlying psychology — just delivered through different channels.
